Body of Divinity
BOD-ee uhv di-VIN-i-tee
theological work
From body (a complete and ordered whole) and divinity (the science of God, theology); a settled term for a systematic exposition of the whole of Christian doctrine.

📖 Biblical Definition

A “body of divinity” is a full and orderly treatment of the whole counsel of God, setting forth in connected form the doctrines of Scripture concerning God, man, sin, Christ, salvation, the church, and the last things. The phrase belongs especially to the Reformed and Puritan tradition, which produced many such works, the most beloved being Thomas Watson’s A Body of Divinity, lectures upon the Westminster Shorter Catechism, prized for their warmth and quaint, pungent illustration. The aim of a body of divinity is not bare information but the knowledge of God unto godliness; it follows the conviction that doctrine and life are not divided, that sound theology is the handmaid of holiness, and that the catechized believer is the established believer. Such works typically follow the order of a confession or catechism, expounding each head of doctrine, answering objections, and pressing application upon the conscience. The dictionary commends the body of divinity as the proper fruit of a church that takes the whole counsel of God seriously: not a few favorite themes endlessly repeated, but the entire system of truth taught, learned, confessed, and obeyed. To know a little of everything God has revealed, and that little well ordered, is the laborer’s armory and the believer’s stability.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A complete and ordered exposition of the whole of Christian doctrine; especially Thomas Watson’s beloved Puritan exposition of the Westminster Shorter Catechism.

expand to see more

BODY OF DIVINITY, a systematic treatment of the entire compass of Christian doctrine.

From divinity, the older English term for theology, the science of God and divine things.

Typically follows the order of a confession or catechism through each head of doctrine.

The most cherished example is Thomas Watson’s, lectures on the Westminster Shorter Catechism.

Designed not for mere knowledge but for the knowledge of God unto godliness and stability.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 20:27 — "For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God."

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Tit 2:1 — "But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:"

1Ti 4:16 — "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Systematic theology is dismissed as cold or divisive by an age that prizes vague spirituality over ordered truth.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the whole counsel of God is to be declared, learned, and held in an ordered form. A body of divinity stands against the modern preference for a handful of comforting themes endlessly repeated, and against the notion that doctrine divides while experience unites. Watson and his fellows knew that the most affectionate, practical, and stable Christians are the best instructed ones.

Where a corruption presses, it is the false opposition of head and heart—the suspicion that systematic doctrine quenches devotion. The Puritan body of divinity is the standing refutation: its pages are at once rigorous and warm, doctrinal and devotional, pressing every truth home upon the conscience. To know God systematically is not to know Him coldly; it is to love Him with the mind as well as the heart, as the great commandment requires.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The term joins the idea of a complete body with the old word for theology, naming an ordered whole of Christian truth.

expand to see more

English body — a complete, organized whole, used of a connected system.

English divinity — the science of God, theology, from Latin divinitas.

The phrase parallels Latin corpus theologiae, a body or corpus of theology.

Akin in aim to the catechism and the confession, but fuller in exposition.

Watson, Ussher, and others gave the title to their systematic works.

Usage

"A new believer is often pointed to a body of divinity to gain the whole frame of Christian doctrine."

"Pastors recommend Watson’s as a warm, quotable companion to the Shorter Catechism."

"The phrase is used to distinguish a complete systematic work from a treatise on one doctrine."
